A de novo heterozygous pathogenic variant in the NIPBL gene was detected, consistent with Cornelia de Lange syndrome 1.

A de novo heterozygous variant of uncertain significance in the KMT2D gene and a paternally inherited intragenic deletion in the BAZSB gene were detected, possibly related to this patient's phenotype.

schemas.name: p3_geneDesc
schemas.content: The NIPBL gene encodes a protein forming a dimer with MAU2 as a cohesin loader complex that is essential for sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome condensation, and DNA repair.

schemas.name: p3_diseaseDesc
schemas.content: Defects in the NIPBL gene may cause autosomal dominant Cornelia de Lange syndrome 1 (OMIM: 122470), which is a multisystem disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency, psychomotor delay, intellectual disability, hirsutism, upper limb defects, congenital heart defects, gastrointestinal dysfunction, hearing loss, and behavioral abnormalities. Additional features may include microcephaly, cleft or high-arched palate, seizures, genital abnormalities, ophthalmologic abnormalities, renal anomalies, diaphragmatic hernia, cryptorchidism, and hypospadias. The severity is variable, ranging from relatively mild to severe presentations with widely syndactyly), gastrointestinal problems, genitourinary anomalies, and behavioral abnormalities as autism and self-injurious behaviors. Many patients have features that do not fit neatly into one of the four categories. Facial features may include microbrachycephaly, synophrys, long eyelashes, ptosis, short nasal bridge with anteverted nares, cleft or high-arched palate, thin upper lip, downturned corners of mouth, dental anomalies, and micrognathia.

schemas.name: p3_variantDetails
schemas.content:
• (GRCh38/chr5:36985658CacC - NM_133433.4

• The c.2479del (p.R827Gfs*20) variant in the NIPBL gene has been described as pathogenic in ClinVar (ID: 950707). This variant has been previously reported as de novo in individuals with Cornelia de Lange syndrome (PMID: 20824774, 36913886).

• This variant has not been observed in the gnomAD v4 dataset.

• This frameshift variant is located in exon 16 of 47 and predicted to be deleterious.

schemas.name: p4_geneDesc
schemas.content: The KMT2D gene encodes a histone methyltransferase that methylates the lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4) as part of the chromatin remodeling machinery involved in transcriptional regulation and DNA repair.

schemas.name: p4_diseaseDesc
schemas.content: Defects in the KMT2D gene may cause autosomal dominant Kabuki syndrome 1 (OMIM: 147920), which is characterized by postnatal dwarfism, mild to moderate intellectual disability, distinctive facial features (including eversion of the lateral third of the lower eyelids, wide-arched eyebrows, large protruding/cupped earlobes, short columella with broad/ depressed nasal tip), abnormal hand/finger pads, and musculoskeletal anomalies (short fifth metacarpal/finger pads). Some patients may also manifest congenital heart defects (coarctation of the aorta, atrial or ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, hypoplastic left heart, tetralogy of Fallot), cleft lip/palate, widely spaced teeth, hypodontia, congenital hypothyroidism, gastrointestinal and genitourinary anomalies (horseshoe kidney, renal hypoplasia, vesicoureteral reflux, cyptorchidism), and/or skeletal abnormalities (joint dislocation, hip dysplasia, scoliosis, vertebral anomalies). Growth retardation is usually postnatal in onset, although some individuals may have prenatal growth retardation. Defects in the KMT2D gene may also cause autosomal dominant short stature, developmental delay, and congenital heart defects with or without bone marrow failure and susceptibility to infection (OMIM: 617186), which is characterized by obstetric atresia, athelia or hypoplastic nipples, lacrimal duct anomalies, hearing loss, external ear malformations, short stature, skeletal anomalies (brachydactyly, clinodactyly, pectus excavatum/carinatum, vertebral and rib fusion), congenital heart defects (atrial septal defect, mitral valve prolapse, patent foramen ovale), decreased susceptibility to infection, and/or hematologic abnormalities (neutropenia, pancytopenia, bone marrow hypoplasia, thrombocytopenia). Additional features may include growth retardation, developmental delay, and intellectual disability.

schemas.name: p4_variantDetails
schemas.content:
• (GRCh38/chr12:49051731G>C - NM_003482.4

• The c.1952C>G (p.S651W) variant in the KMT2D gene has not been described in ClinVar.

• This variant has not been observed in the gnomAD v4 dataset.

• This missense variant occurs at a residue with low evolutionary conservation, and is predicted to be inconclusive (REVEL = 0.21), AlphaMissense = 0.239, CADD = 20.4).

schemas.name: p5_geneDesc
schemas.content: The BAZ2B gene encodes a member of the bromodomain family and is potentially involved in transcriptional activation through chromatin remodeling.

schemas.name: p5_diseaseDesc
schemas.content: Defects in the BAZ2B gene may cause autosomal dominant BAZ2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID: 37877213, 31983221). The clinical features of the BAZ2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder are highly variable, with additional clinical features are highly variable, including growth delay, nonspecific craniofacial dysmorphism often with macrocephaly or microcephaly, abnormal brain imaging, vision issues (strabismus, myopia, hyperopia), hearing loss, feeding difficulties, seizures, hypotonia, sleep disturbances, and autism spectrum disorder. The association between BAZ2B and neurodevelopmental defects is supported by a limited number of affected individuals. Further clinical and genetic studies are warranted to better define disease onset, inheritance, and genotype-phenotype correlations.

schemas.name: p6_geneDesc
schemas.content: The KCNQ1 gene encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel that functions in the repolarization phase of the cardiac action potential.

schemas.name: p6_diseaseDesc
schemas.content: Defects in the KCNQ1 gene may cause autosomal dominant long QT syndrome 1 (OMIM: 192500), which is characterized by a prolonged QT interval at resting heart rate and a high risk of sudden cardiac death (typically at rest or during sleep). Defects in the KCNQ1 gene may also cause autosomal dominant short QT syndrome 2 (OMIM: 609621), which is characterized by episodes of rapid/irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation), torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, syncope, or sudden death without demonstrable cardiac abnormalities except for a shortened QT interval. Clinical findings proposed to be loss-of-function or dominant-negative for long QT syndrome 1 and gain-of-function for short QT syndrome 2 and 3 (PMID: 932295, 12572225, 3580063, 35861379). Defects in the KCNQ1 gene may also cause autosomal recessive Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome 1 (OMIM: 220400), which is characterized by episodes of rapid/irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation, torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, syncope), or sudden death without demonstrable cardiac abnormalities, and congenital deafness. The disease mechanism is proposed to be loss-of-function or dominant-negative for long QT syndrome 1 and gain-of-function for short QT syndromes 2 and 3 (PMID: 932295, 12572225, 3580063, 35861379).

schemas.name: p6_variantDetails
schemas.content:
• (GRCh38/chr11:2768881C>T - NM_000218.3

• The c.1552C>T (p.R518*) variant in the KCNQ1 gene has been described as pathogenic in ClinVar (ID: 3131). This variant has been previously reported in individuals with Long QT syndrome 1 (PMID: 9880418*, 24525245*, 36128627).

• This variant has been observed in gnomAD with a frequency of < 0.05%.

• This stop-gain variant is located in exon 12 of 16 and predicted to be deleterious.

schemas.name: p7_methodologyContent
schemas.content:
Genomic DNA was fragmented and indexed to prepare individual libraries. The libraries were purified and pooled for sequence analysis using the Illumina NovaSeq/NextSeq platform after paired end reads. Internal quality measures were employed to ensure sample integrity.

Data analysis and interpretation of sequence reads was conducted using the Baylor Genetics analytics pipeline. Data is aligned to the human reference genome build GRCh38 using the Illumina Dragen BioIT Platform. Variant calling is performed using the Illumina Dragen haplotype-based variant calling software and depth calling (CNV tool). For Number and depth of coverage (DOC) metrics used to support calls are run with analysis modifications from Baylor Genetics. Short tandem repeat calling is performed using the Illumina Expansion Hunter tool. The automated variant interpretation from ExpansionHunter relies on variant annotation such as Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) with proprietary algorithms and open-source data such as gnomAD, EVS (Exome Variant Server), ClinVar, and professional publications and knowledgebases such as HGMD (Human Gene Mutation Database), ClinGen consensus guidelines (reference 1) and patient phenotypes.

Variants are classified as pathogenic if specific PVS1, Multiple (>2) strong lines of evidence (PS) dependent upon Probe Amplification (MLPA), or another method. If no CNV is detected by NGS that it does not meet internal quality standards or are within highly ambiguous or homologous genomic regions, CNV interpretations are not included for those genes. Sample mix-ups, consanguinity, or the presence of closely related pseudogenes. Small deletions or insertions larger than 25bp, low-level mosaic variants, structural rearrangements in the non-coding or intergenic regions, or variants with unusual or complex variant types being analyzed include sequencing variants and CNV in nuclear genes and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and short tandem repeat (STR) in nuclear genes. Methods for CNV, GJB2 (STR), mtDNA, and CNV may be provided individually for each individual within the trio (parents and proband), resulting in coverage reported when greater than 5 Mb. Sensitivity of detection is decreased for mtDNA sequencing variants and CNVs at heteroplasmy levels lower than 10%. Pseudogene analysis is provided only for parental reporting for the human reference genome build GRCh38, repeat tandem repeats within the genomic regions of following genes: ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, ATXN7, ATXN10, ATXN1, CACNA1A, CSTB, DMPK, FGF14, FMR1, FXN, HTT, JPH3, NOP56, NOTCH2NLC, PABPN1, PHOX2B, PPP2R2B, RFC1, TBP, and TCF4. Sensitivity of detection may be reported when greater than 1-5 base deletions reported in the genotype regions of the proband report contains results of genes related to the patient's clinical phenotype. Variants relevant to the phenotype are reported as Positive Proband Findings. Incidental findings for genes with highly actionable incidental findings (VUS) (Benign and likely benign variants are not reported. This interpretation is based on the clinical information provided by the referring institution and our current understanding of the genome at the time of reporting. Additional methodologies may be used to aid in variant interpretation. Results in the report should be carefully correlated to the individual's clinical findings by the referring physician.

schemas.name: p8_limitationsContent
schemas.content: If elected, secondary findings including pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants in genes included in the ACMG secondary findings recommendations, or other findings determined to be severe and medically significant (incidental findings), will be reported. Specific genes subject to secondary findings reporting include: ACTA2, ACTC1, ANK2, APOB, ATP7B, BRCA1, BRCA2, BTD, CACNA1S, CALM1, CALM2, CALM3, CASSR2, COL3A1, DSC2, DSG2, DSP, ENG, FBN1, FKR1, RB2, GLA, HFE, HNF1A, HNF4A, KCNH2, KCNQ1, LDLR, LMNA, MAX, MEN1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, MYBPC3, MYH11, MYH7, MYL2, MYL3, NF2, OTC, PALB2, PMS2, POLD1, POLE, PRKAG2, RB1, RET, RPE65, RYR2, SDHAF2, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SMAD3, SMAD4, STK11, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, TMEM127, TMEM43, TNNI3, TNNT2, TP53, TPM1, TRDN, TSC1, TSC2, TTN, TTR, VHL, and WT1. Variants unrelated to the patient's phenotype in genes with a high risk of medically actionable and clinical significance will be reported if elected.

schemas.name: p8_limitationsText
schemas.content: The interpretation of nucleotide changes is based on our current understanding of the specific genes. This interpretation may change over time if new information about these genes becomes available. Potential diagnostic errors include sample mix-ups, genetic variants that interfere with analysis, incorrect assignment of biological parentage, or other sources. Please contact a genetic counselor at Baylor Genetics if there is reason to suspect that a variant has been misinterpreted.
